Description: An isolated typographical or spelling error that is objectively incorrect.
Example: "Unietd states" instead of "United States"; "Misisipi"

Description: Clashes in terminology or spelling referring to the same entity (neither is incorrect by itself).
Example: "USA" vs. "United states"

Description: Inconsistent capitalization referring to the same entity.
Example: "james smith" vs. "James Smith" or "John Doe"; "ID-123" vs. "id-234"

Description: Values that represent the same semantic data but fail to conform to a standardized syntax or layout.
Clashes in specific punctuation marks used, or the presence of leading/trailing empty spaces.
Example: "123-456" vs. "123---456" (en dash vs em dash); " james smith " vs. "james smith"

Description: Broad differences in how numbers are formatted and stored within a single column.
Example: Percentage numbers (15%) mixed with floating numbers (0.15).

Description: Out-of-domain values placed in the wrong column.
Example: Phone numbers in a "Name" column; a name in a "Salary" column.

Description: Values that deviate significantly from the mathematical or statistical distribution of the bulk of the data.
Example: A salary of $1,000,000 resting three standard deviations from the mean.

Description: Unavailable values during data entry, including true NULLs or disguised/dummy NULLs.
Example: A required phone number field filled with "9999-999999".

Description: Multiple distinct values or attributes are improperly entered into a single free-form field instead of being split across columns.
Example: Entering "J. Smith 12.02.70 New York" into a single "Name" field.

Description: Values across different columns factually contradict one another based on real-world logic or embedded data.
Example: Country => Capital city is incorrect; End-date < Start-date; First Name + Last Name do not match the Full Name column.

Description: A violation of strict, known dependencies between specific attributes within a dataset.
Example: Zip code does not map to the correct State.

Description: Numerical fields within the same row fail to satisfy an expected mathematical formula or derivation.
Example: Unit-price * quantity != total-price.

Description: Data that breaches complex, explicit internal business logic rather than standard structural constraints.
Example: Two employees with the exact same Title and Location earning different amounts when strict internal rules forbid it.

Description: Numerical fields fail to satisfy expected mathematical aggregations down a column.
Example: Numbers in a "Revenue" column do not sum up to the value printed in the final "Total" row.

Description: Distinct rows that refer to the identical real-world entity (exact duplicates), often caused by repeated ingestion.
Example: Two identical rows representing the exact same transaction.

Description: The same real-world entity is described by conflicting temporal or descriptive values across multiple separate rows.
Example: A single employee having two separate profile records in the HR table with differing birthdates or spellings of their name.

Description: Reference key issues, broken links, or violations of referential integrity across parent-child tables.
Example: A record is assigned to "Department 127", but Department 127 does not exist in the parent Departments table.

Description: Schema-level homonyms (identical names for different objects) or synonyms (different names for the exact same object) across databases.
Example: When merging tables, one system uses CustomerID while the other uses ClientNumber.

Description: Differences in the underlying data formatting, scaling, or interpretation across disparate sources being merged.
Example: Sales recorded in USD in one system and EUR in another; Gender coded as 0/1 in Table A versus M/F in Table B.
